passages.t: Comfort for God's people, and a voice in the wilderness
passages.happening:
A new voice: ‘Comfort, comfort My people,’ says your God (verse 1). ‘Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and proclaim to her that her forced labor has been completed; her iniquity has been pardoned’ (verse 2). She has received double for all her sins.

A voice calls, ‘Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness; make a straight highway for our God in the desert’ (verse 3). Every valley will be raised and every mountain made low (verse 4), ‘And the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all humanity together will see it’ (verse 5).

A voice says, Cry out. What shall be cried? ‘All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field’ (verse 6). ‘The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever’ (verse 8).

Zion is told to go up on a high mountain as a herald of good news, and to say to the cities of Judah, ‘Here is your God’ (verse 9). The Lord GOD comes with might (verse 10). ‘He tends His flock like a shepherd; He gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart. He gently leads the nursing ewes’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
From chapter 40 the tone and the horizon change. Jerusalem fell to the Babylonians in 587 or 586 BC. The temple was burned, the monarchy ended, and many of Judah's leading families were taken to Babylonia, where they lived for decades. In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia captured Babylon, and in 539 or 538 BC he allowed exiled peoples, including the Judeans, to go home and rebuild. Chapters 40 to 55 speak into the last years of the exile, looking toward that release.

How the book came to address that situation is one of the classic questions of the study of the Old Testament, and it arises here because the setting changes so sharply. The traditional view holds that Isaiah of Jerusalem was given these words in the eighth century for a generation not yet born. Most critical scholars assign chapters 40 to 55 to an anonymous prophet of the exile, often called Second Isaiah, because these chapters assume the fall of Jerusalem as past and speak of Cyrus as already on the scene. Many in both camps now read the book as a deliberate whole. The book page sets out the positions more fully.

The word comfort, nacham, answers the cry of Lamentations that Jerusalem had no one to comfort her. The road through the wilderness recalls the exodus: God himself will lead his people home, and a highway will be built for him. The God who comes with power also carries the lambs close to his heart.
passages.later: All four Gospels take up verse 3 for John the Baptist, ‘A voice of one calling in the wilderness’ (Mark 1:3; compare Luke 3:4-6). Peter quotes verses 6 to 8: ‘the word of the Lord stands forever’ (1 Peter 1:25). And Lamentations had cried that the city had no one to comfort her (Lamentations 1:2).
passages.asks: The first words of the second half of the book are comfort and pardon. Ask whether you have heard God speak tenderly to you, after a hard season. And ask what in your life is grass, and what is the word that stands forever.

passages.t: To whom will you compare God?
passages.happening:
‘Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, or marked off the heavens with the span of his hand?’ (verse 12). Who weighed the mountains? ‘Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or informed Him as His counselor?’ (verse 13).

‘Surely the nations are like a drop in a bucket’ (verse 15). Lebanon's forests would not be enough fuel for his altar (verse 16). All the nations are as nothing before him (verse 17).

‘To whom will you liken God? To what image will you compare Him?’ (verse 18). To an idol a craftsman casts and overlays with gold, or carves from wood that will not rot, so it will not fall over (verses 19-20)?

‘He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth; its dwellers are like grasshoppers’ (verse 22). He brings princes to nothing; as soon as they take root, he blows on them and they wither (verses 23-24). ‘To whom will you liken Me, or who is My equal?’ asks the Holy One (verse 25). ‘Lift up your eyes on high: Who created all these? He leads forth the starry host by number; He calls each one by name’ (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The exiles lived in Babylon, among the gods of the world's greatest empire. In Babylon's great festivals, the images of the gods were carried in procession along broad ceremonial roads. Isaiah answers with questions. Who measured the oceans in his palm? Who taught God? Who can be compared with him?

The mockery of idols is sharp. The rich man's idol is cast in metal and covered in gold. The poor man's is carved from good wood and propped up so it will not topple. Either way, a god that has to be held up cannot hold anyone up.

The stars, which Israel's law warned against worshiping (Deuteronomy 4:19), are in verse 26 an army God leads out by number and calls by name. Not one of them is missing. The first hearers, small and scattered among the empires, were told that the God of Israel sits above the circle of the earth and counts the stars.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 13 in praise of God's wisdom: ‘Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?’ (Romans 11:34). And a psalm says, ‘He determines the number of the stars; He calls them each by name’ (Psalm 147:4).
passages.asks: The prophet asks who can be compared with God. Ask what you are comparing God to, quietly, when you doubt him. And ask what idol in your life has to be propped up so it will not fall.

passages.t: Those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength
passages.happening:
God asks why Jacob and Israel say that their way is hidden from the LORD, ‘and my claim is ignored by my God’ (verse 27).

‘Do you not know? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He will not grow tired or weary; His understanding is beyond searching out’ (verse 28).

‘He gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the weak’ (verse 29). Even young men grow tired and stumble (verse 30). ‘But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint’ (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The exiles' complaint is honest: God has lost track of them; their case has been dropped. After decades in Babylon, it felt true.

The answer is not a scolding. It is the reminder that the God who counts the stars does not grow tired, and that he gives strength to the faint. Waiting on the LORD, in Hebrew, carries the sense of hoping in him, leaning one's weight on what he will do.

The three verbs at the end, mount up, run, walk, move from the dramatic to the ordinary. Strength to fly on great days, to run when needed, and to keep walking without fainting on long ordinary ones. The first hearers had a long walk home ahead of them.
passages.later: A psalm prays the same waiting: ‘Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD’ (Psalm 27:14). And Paul writes, ‘we do not lose heart’ (2 Corinthians 4:16).
passages.asks: The exiles said their way was hidden from God. Ask whether you have said the same. And ask which of the three you most need today: strength to fly, to run, or simply to keep walking.
